# pact-identity — the contract every port implements

One library, several homes: a Rust core (`crates/pact-identity`) compiled to WebAssembly for the
browser, Cloudflare Workers and Node (`crates/pact-identity-wasm`, loaders in `js/`), compiled
natively for the `pact` CLI (`crates/pact`), and an independent Go port (`go/`) that the vectors tie
to the first. This file is the boundary all of them present: **bytes in, JSON out**, no state, the
same names, the same shapes. The specification is `pact-protocol/SPEC.md` (2.2.4) and, where
the spec leaves a byte to the implementer, `pact-protocol/vectors/lib/*.mjs` — the seed library —
which every port must match byte for byte on the vectors in
`pact-protocol/vectors/pact-2.0-vectors.json` and in SPEC.md Appendix B.

**This file is generated.** `contract/contract.json` is the source: 51 functions, each with
the shape of its arguments, the shape of its answer and the error codes it may fail with, over the
domain types they are assembled from. `js/parity.mjs` validates every answer of BOTH ports against
that same file, so these tables and the gate cannot describe different contracts — which they did:
the tables said `card_decode` answers with a `leaf` while one port had stopped sending one, and said
nothing at all about `decide`'s `tool`, which was `null` in Rust and absent in Go. The prose around
the tables is `contract/CONTRACT.template.md` and is written by hand.

## 0. Conventions

- **Bytes in JSON** are base64url without padding (`b64url`), and an answer always spells them so.
  An argument's bytes are read forgiving the padding and the standard alphabet's `+` and `/`, and
  nothing else: whitespace of any kind, any other character outside the alphabet, `=` anywhere but
  the end, and a last character with a spare bit set are `{"error": "parse", "why": "not
  base64url"}`. Every string a port reads that it did not write itself — a card's certificate, a
  chain in a peer's plaintext, a pin's leaf, a held key, a vault's salt, nonce and ciphertext — is
  read by the same rule and refused in its function's words. One list of cases,
  `js/b64url-arguments.json`, holds both ports to it. The members of an envelope that travelled are
  read by a stricter rule (§5). The vector file alone uses hex.
- **Instants** in JSON are RFC 3339 UTC strings with second precision (`"2026-09-13T12:00:00Z"`);
  `ts` and `exp` inside an envelope header stay integer Unix seconds, as the spec says.
- **Keys**: a private key is PKCS #8 DER; a public key is SubjectPublicKeyInfo DER. Algorithms are
  `"ed25519"` and `"p256"`. A **fingerprint** is `"sha256:" + b64url(SHA-256(SPKI))`; a **key id** is
  the 32 raw bytes of that hash. A key of any other algorithm — RSA, P-384, a bare X25519 key, an
  Ed25519 key whose AlgorithmIdentifier carries parameters — is refused where it is read, as a key or
  inside a certificate or a request: `{"error": "unsupported", "why": "unsupported key type <OID>"}`,
  the OID the key's AlgorithmIdentifier names first (a function that answers a refusal as its result
  carries the same words: chain rule 1, `csr_check`, `card_decode`). The seed's `parse` refuses it in
  the same words.
- **Every function returns one JSON object.** Success shapes are listed per function. Failure is
  `{"error": "<code>", "why": "<one line>"}`, where `code` is a spec error where one applies
  (`envelope_invalid`, `chain_required`, `certificate_renewed`, `bad_request`, `pending_approval`) and
  otherwise one of `parse`, `profile`, `unsupported`, `key`, `vault`, `internal`. Ports never throw
  across the boundary.
- **A member that is absent is not a member that is empty.** Absent answers `{"error": "bad_request",
  "why": "<name> is required"}` naming the member the caller left out; present but unusable — `""`,
  bytes that will not decode, a string where an object belongs — answers what is wrong with the value
  (`parse`/`"not base64url"`, a parser's own words). A port whose zero value and missing value are
  the same thing loses this distinction, and both have: `{"spki": ""}` once read as "spki is
  required" in one port and as a truncated DER in the other. The JSON literal `null` counts as absent.
- **A member of the wrong JSON type is refused, never read as absent** — an optional one too, which is
  where the ports parted: one read `"serial": 7` as no serial and drew a random one, `"guest": "yes"`
  as not a guest and `"exp": "7"` as ts + 600, and the other refused each. A base64url member that is
  not a string answers `{"error": "parse", "why": "not base64url"}`, as bytes that will not decode
  do; any other answers `bad_request` in words that name it — `<name> is required`, the words its
  absence gets, unless the function has more particular ones (`first_line is a line number from 1`).
  An integer is a number written without a fraction or an exponent, and not `-0`: `365.0` and `-0`
  are not a number of days, although JavaScript reads both as one.
- **The order a function reads its members is part of its answer.** When several required members are
  missing, the one named is the first the function needs, and both ports read them in the same order.
- **A member a function does not declare is refused**, before any member is read: `{"error":
  "bad_request", "why": "<fn> takes no member \"<m>\""}`, naming the first such member in sorted
  order. A function declares the members its `params` list, and no others. This holds the arguments
  object itself; the objects inside a member (an envelope, a node state, a pin) are read for the
  members they need and not held to their schemas' `additionalProperties`, because a host's typed
  port, which decodes them into fixed structs, cannot see a member it has no field for either.
- **`why` is part of the answer.** Two ports refusing the same call in different words is a
  divergence, not a detail: it is what a person debugging reads, and what a caller's test asserts. No
  `why` may be a library's own error text — one port cannot reproduce another library's wording.
- **Half a surrogate pair is refused before anything else.** Arguments holding a `\u` escape of half
  a UTF-16 surrogate pair (a high one not followed by a low one, or a low one alone) answer
  `{"error": "bad_request", "why": "args: a string holds half of a UTF-16 surrogate pair"}` from
  every function, before the arguments are read: one JSON parser refuses such text and another reads
  it as U+FFFD, and a port must not answer by its parser's choice.
- **So is what one JSON parser refuses and another reads**, next: a number that is infinite as a
  double (`1e400`) answers `{"error": "bad_request", "why": "args: a number is outside the range of a
  double"}`, and arrays and objects nested more than 127 deep, the arguments object counted, `args:
  nested more than 127 deep` — whichever comes first in the text. JSON that travels as text — an
  envelope's header and body, a manifest, a line of `messages.jsonl`, a vault's plaintext — holding
  either is text that is not JSON, answered as each function answers that. RFC 8785, in which a
  header is written, has no infinite number. Arguments that do not parse at all answer `args is a
  JSON object`.
- **`version` is the one exception.** It describes the port, not a rule, so its answer differs and
  nothing compares it.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `version` | — | `spec`: string, `crate`?: string, `module`?: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | The build, not a rule: `spec` is the version of `pact-protocol/SPEC.md` the port implements and is the same everywhere; the other member names the port's own release, so the answers differ and nothing compares them. |
- The Wasm boundary takes `&str` JSON and `&[u8]` DER and returns `String` JSON. The Go port exposes
  the same functions as Go functions on `[]byte`/`string` returning structs, plus a `pact-identity-go`
  binary that reads JSON requests on stdin, one per line (`{"fn": "<name>", "args": {...}}`), and
  writes one JSON answer per line, so the JavaScript suites can aim the same cases at both ports
  through one process per run.

| `key_from_seed` | `alg`: Alg, `seed`: Seed32 | `alg`: Alg, `pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `spki`: Spki, `fingerprint`: Fingerprint<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` | An Ed25519 seed is used directly; a P-256 scalar is the seed mod n, with 0 → 1 (the seed library's `keys.mjs`). Written for the vectors, and production API since SPEC §2.1: it is how a wallet turns a derived seed into its root. |
| `prf_salt` | — | `salt`: Seed32, `infos`: [string]<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | SPEC §2.1's fixed PRF input, `SHA-256("pact/vault/1")`, and the three `info` strings. A call rather than a constant a caller copies, so the bytes live in one place and the vectors prove them. |
| `derive_seed` | `prf`: Seed32, `info`: string | `seed`: Seed32<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | `HKDF-SHA256(ikm = prf, salt = "", info, L = 32)`. **Refuses an `info` outside the three, and a `prf` that is not 32 bytes.** Both refusals are the point rather than hygiene: a mistyped domain separator would otherwise return 32 perfectly good bytes and silently derive an identity belonging to nobody, which is the one failure the derived-root design exists to prevent. |
| `public_key` | `pkcs8`: Pkcs8 | `alg`: Alg, `spki`: Spki, `fingerprint`: Fingerprint<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` |  |

`sign` is the leaf key's one signing primitive; a host signs exactly four structures with it
(SPEC §13.5). The CLI exposes no signing command and no pass-through to `call`, so there is no other
use to make of it there — by omission, not by a guard: nobody should add a `pact sign` believing one
exists.

So `address_guard`, chain rule 5, `csr_check`, `ledger_check` and the export's endpoint column refuse one as not the normal form. |
| `address_guard` | `endpoint`: string, `self_endpoint`?: string, `guest`?: boolean | `ok`: true<br>or `ok`: false, `why`: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | Refuses a host that is a loopback, link-local, private, unspecified or CGNAT literal (`localhost`, `*.localhost`, `127/8`, `10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`, `169.254/16`, `100.64/10`, `0.0.0.0`, `::1`, `::`, `fc00::/7`, `fe80::/10`, deprecated site-local `fec0::/10`, NAT64's local-use `64:ff9b:1::/48`), an IPv6 literal that EMBEDS such an IPv4 address — IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible `::/96`, NAT64 `64:ff9b::/96`, 6to4 `2002::/16` — because a translator dials the address inside (`[64:ff9b::7f00:1]` is loopback on a NAT64 network, and a literal has no name to resolve, so this is the whole guard), and, for a guest, an endpoint equal to `self_endpoint`. DNS resolution is the host's; `ip_is_private` is exposed so the host applies the same predicate to what it resolves. |
| `ip_is_private` | `ip`: string | `private`: boolean<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | The predicate `address_guard` applies to a literal host, for the host to apply to what it resolves. One leading `[` and one trailing `]` are dropped, as a URL writes an IPv6 host, and no more. An IPv6 literal with a zone id (`fe80::1%eth0`) is private whatever its address: a zone is an interface scope (RFC 4007 §6), which no global address carries. Text that is no address is not private: an empty zone, and a zone on an IPv4 address, are no address, as Go's `netip` reads them. |

Serial numbers: random 8 bytes by default; when `serial` is supplied it is used as given, which is
how the vectors reproduce (`serial = SHA-256("serial/" + label)[0..8]`). Times encode as UTCTime
before 2050 and GeneralizedTime from 2050; the root's `not_after` is always `99991231235959Z`.
Signature algorithm OIDs, extension order, criticality, key-usage bit encoding and every other byte
follow `x509.mjs` — the vector certificates must reproduce exactly from the same inputs.

The wallet's monotonic rule is the caller's: `not_before` = the later of (now − 1 h) and (previous
leaf's `not_before` + 1 s); the core enforces `not_after − not_before ≤ 398 d` and refuses otherwise.

## 3. Certificate signing requests (PKCS #10, SPEC §9)

A CSR is `CertificationRequest ::= SEQUENCE { certificationRequestInfo, signatureAlgorithm, signature }`
with an exact profile of its own: `version` 0; `subject` one UTF-8 `commonName`; the host's SPKI;
`attributes [0]` holding exactly one `extensionRequest` (`1.2.840.113549.1.9.14`) whose value is one
`subjectAltName` extension (non-critical) with exactly one URI and optionally one `dNSName` equal to
its host; the signature is by the CSR's own key with that key's own algorithm (proof of possession).
Strict DER, nothing trailing.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `csr_new` | `cn`: string, `host_pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `endpoint`: string, `dns_name`?: string | `der`: Csr<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` |  |
| `csr_check` | `der`: Csr, `root_spkis`?: [Spki] | `ok`: true, `cn`: string, `spki`: Spki, `fingerprint`: Fingerprint, `alg`: Alg, `endpoint`: string, `dns_name`: string\|null<br>or `ok`: false, `why`: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | Refuses a bad signature (no proof of possession), a key equal to any root in `root_spkis` (the root-key refusal), an endpoint that is not normal https, an endpoint the address guard refuses. `root_spkis` absent is no roots; present and unreadable is an error, never "no roots to refuse against". |
| `issue_from_csr` | `csr`: Csr, `root_cn`: string, `root_spkis`?: [Spki], `now`: InstantIn, `previous_not_before`?: InstantIn, `valid_days`?: integer, `root_pkcs8`: Pkcs8 | `der`: CertDer, `endpoint`: string, `not_before`: Instant, `not_after`: Instant<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` | `csr_check` first — with the issuing root added to `root_spkis` — then `build_leaf` under the monotonic rule. `valid_days` absent is 365; an explicit 0 is refused. |
| `issue_tbs_from_csr` | `csr`: Csr, `root_cn`: string, `root_spkis`?: [Spki], `now`: InstantIn, `previous_not_before`?: InstantIn, `valid_days`?: integer, `root_spki`: Spki | `tbs`: Tbs, `sig_alg`: SigAlg, `endpoint`: string, `not_before`: Instant, `not_after`: Instant<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` | As `issue_from_csr`, for the seam: assembled with `assemble_leaf`. |

### 3.1 Signing requests (SPEC §9.1)

A host asks a web wallet for a leaf with a form POSTed by top-level navigation, carrying a
`SigningRequest`: the CSR, `renew` or `move`, the root it expects, where the answer goes, an opaque
`state`, what the host calls itself, the validity it asks for, and when the request expires. The
wallet runs `signing_request_check` on it before a person sees anything, and answers by navigating
to `redirect` with `#chain=<leaf>.<root>&state=<state>` or `#error=<code>&state=<state>`. The
check is stateless: nothing of a request is kept.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `signing_request_check` | `request`: `{…}`, `origin`: string, `now`: InstantIn, `root_spkis`?: [Spki] | `ok`: true, `csr`: Csr, `redirect`: string, `purpose`: renew\|move, `valid_days`: integer<br>or `ok`: false, `why`: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | What a web wallet decides about a host's signing request before a person sees it. The arguments first: `request` absent or not an object, `origin` absent or not a string, `now` absent (each `<name> is required`), `now` unreadable (`parse`), `root_spkis` unreadable — these are errors. Everything about the request itself is `{ok: false, why}`, the first thing wrong, in this order: a member a request does not carry (the first in sorted order: `a signing request does not carry <m>`); a member that is not a string (`<m> is a string, as a form carries it`) or over its bound (`<m> is longer than <n>`), in the order of SigningRequest's members; a required member absent or empty (`<m> is required`); an `origin` empty or `null` (`the request has no origin: a wallet answers only the origin that asked`); the redirect — not ASCII without spaces or backslashes (`the redirect is not an absolute URL`), a fragment (`the redirect carries a fragment`), not `https://` or `http://` (`the redirect is not https, or http to a loopback host`), userinfo (`the redirect carries userinfo`), a host not in lower-case normal form — IPv6 hex in lower case, a name of labels none of which is empty (`the redirect's host is not in normal form`), a port that is not 1–65535 without a leading zero (`the redirect's port is not in normal form`), `http` to a host that is not `localhost`, a dotted quad in `127.0.0.0/8` in normal form, or `[::1]` (`the redirect is not https, or http to a loopback host`); the redirect's origin (`scheme://host[:port]`, the default port left out) not equal to `origin` (`the redirect's origin is not the origin that asked`); `expires` not an RFC 3339 UTC instant in the one grammar — upper-case `T` and `Z`, `.` alone before a fraction (`expires is not an RFC 3339 instant`), not after `now` (`the request has expired`), or more than 600 seconds after it (`the request expires more than ten minutes ahead`); `purpose` not `renew` or `move` (`purpose is renew or move`; `signup` is not taken from a host); `valid_days` not a whole number 1–398 without a leading zero (`valid_days is a whole number of days from 1 to 398`); `state` not 43 base64url characters of 32 bytes (`state is 32 bytes, base64url`); `expect_root` not `sha256:` and 43 base64url characters (`expect_root is not a root fingerprint`); `root_cert`, when present, not base64url, not a certificate, not a root of §14.1's profile, or not the root `expect_root` names; `csr` not base64url (`csr is not base64url`); then `csr_check` with `root_spkis`, whose refusal is answered in its words. What stays the wallet's: proving the root against `expect_root` (§2.2), showing the asking origin, the `recipient` as the host's claim, the endpoint, the validity and whether the host is new, and the validity the person chooses. Nothing of the request is kept. |

## 4. Cards (SPEC §3)

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `card_encode` | `fn`: string, `cert`: CertDer, `seal`?: string, `extra`?: [string] | `vcard`: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | Folded per RFC 6350 at 75 octets, CRLF, exactly as the seed's `card.mjs`. Refuses `<fn|seal|extra> carries a control character`: a card is lines, and a line break in anything a caller supplies writes a property of the caller's choosing (SPEC §3). |
| `card_decode` | `vcard`: string, `now`: InstantIn | `fn`: string, `version`: 2, `seal`: string, `cert`: CertDer, `root`: Fingerprint, `endpoint`: string, `expired`: boolean, `ignored`: [string], `bytes`: integer, `leaf`: Certificate<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | Every refusal is `bad_request` with the exact `why` strings of `card.mjs`. An empty `X-PACT-VERSION` names no version (`no X-PACT-VERSION`). `X-PACT-CERT` is read as every string a port did not write is read (§0), so a stray character, whitespace or a spare bit set is `certificate does not parse: not base64url`. |

`card_decode` is intake: it refuses no version, a version it does not implement, zero or several
certificates, a certificate that does not parse, no issuer key identifier or one that is not 32
bytes (it is what `root` is made from, and `root` is what a person is shown), no endpoint or several,
or a validity over 398 days; an expired leaf is reported, not refused. `now` is REQUIRED: it is what
`expired` means, and absent it used to be 1970, so every card answered `expired: false`. The address guard is a separate call
the host makes with its own endpoint in hand.

## 5. Envelopes (SPEC §13)

Suites: `PACT-SEAL-P256` (DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256), HKDF-SHA256, AES-128-GCM) for a P-256 recipient,
`PACT-SEAL-X25519` (DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256), HKDF-SHA256, ChaCha20-Poly1305) for an Ed25519
recipient converted by the RFC 7748 §4.1 and RFC 8032 §5.1.5 maps; a bare X25519 key is no key of
the profile (§0). A suite that is not the recipient key's is `envelope_invalid`, `suite does not fit
the key`. HPKE Base mode, single shot, `info` = `PACT-SEAL-v2`. All-zero DH output refused: a seal to
an Ed25519 key of small order meets one, and is `envelope_invalid`, `all-zero DH output: low-order
point`; an open that meets one does not open. The
header is the AAD, canonicalised per RFC 8785; the signature is over `protected ‖ enc ‖ ct`.

**A member of an envelope has ONE spelling** (SPEC §13.1): unpadded base64url, canonical. `decide`
and `open_result` read `protected`, `enc`, `ct` and `sig` with a reader that refuses everything else —
a character outside the alphabet, padding, whitespace, the standard alphabet's `+` and `/`, a last
character with a spare bit set — because `sig` covers the DECODED bytes and every spelling a reader
forgives is another envelope that verifies. This is NOT the rule for an argument a caller hands the
boundary (§0), which stays forgiving about padding and alphabet; it is the rule for what travels.
An unreadable `protected` is `protected is not JSON`, `enc` or `ct` is `does not open`, and a `sig`
that does not read is no signature and fails as one (`open_result`: `signature`).

**A pin MAY say which leaf it holds** (`leaf_fingerprint`). A small-form envelope names a leaf, and
finding the pin that holds it meant parsing every pinned leaf, for a sender who has proved nothing.
With the member, the match is a string comparison and only the pin that matched is parsed; the match
is held to its own leaf (`parse` / `a pin's leaf_fingerprint is not its leaf's`). Without it the pins
are read as before, so an older host loses only the saving. A pin, a held key or a tombstone that
will not read is an ERROR of the call (`parse`), never a row stepped over: a decision made on state
the node could not read is not a decision.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `suite_for` | `spki`: Spki | `suite`: Suite<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` |  |
| `hpke_seal` | `suite`: Suite, `recipient_spki`: Spki, `info`: string, `aad`?: B64url, `plaintext`: B64url, `ephemeral_seed`?: Seed32 | `enc`: B64url, `ct`: B64url<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `envelope_invalid`, `parse`, `unsupported` | `ephemeral_seed` exists for vectors and the intrusion suite; production callers omit it and the core draws 32 fresh bytes. `aad` absent is empty. |
| `hpke_open` | `suite`: Suite, `recipient_pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `recipient_spki`: Spki, `info`: string, `aad`?: B64url, `enc`: B64url, `ct`: B64url | `plaintext`: B64url<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `envelope_invalid`, `parse`, `unsupported` |  |
| `seal_request` | `recipient_leaf`: CertDer, `sender_pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `form`?: Form, `sender_chain`?: Chain, `msg_id`: string, `ts`: integer, `exp`?: integer, `ephemeral_seed`?: Seed32, `method`?: string, `params`?, `cty`?: string | `protected`: B64url, `enc`: B64url, `ct`: B64url, `sig`: B64url<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `envelope_invalid`, `parse`, `unsupported` | `form` absent is `chain`, which needs `sender_chain`; `method` absent is `tools/call`; `params` absent is `{}`; `exp` absent is `ts + 600`; `cty` absent is a call. |
| `seal_result` | `recipient_spki`: Spki, `sender_pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `form`?: Form, `sender_chain`?: Chain, `msg_id`: string, `ts`: integer, `exp`?: integer, `ephemeral_seed`?: Seed32, `result`?, `error`? | `protected`: B64url, `enc`: B64url, `ct`: B64url, `sig`: B64url<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `envelope_invalid`, `parse`, `unsupported` | Exactly one of `result` and `error`. `cty` is `application/pact-result+json`. |
| `open_result` | `envelope`: ArrivedEnvelope, `my_pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `my_spki`: Spki, `msg_id`: string, `now`: InstantIn, `pins`?: [Pin], `expected_root`?: string, `expected_endpoint`?: string | `ok`: true, `result`?, `error`?, `root`: Fingerprint, `endpoint`: string, `form`: Form, `leaf_update`?: CertDer<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `envelope_invalid`, `parse`, `unsupported` | The caller side of §13.2: opens, requires `result` xor `error` plus one of `chain`/`leaf`, validates the chain to `expected_root` and `expected_endpoint` or finds the named leaf among `pins`, refuses a superseded leaf, verifies `sig`, checks `cty` and `msg_id`. Every refusal of the ENVELOPE is `{"error": "envelope_invalid", "why"}`. `leaf_update` is a leaf newer than the pin, for the host to store. An absent or null `envelope` is the caller's omission, `bad_request` `envelope is required` (CONTRACT §0); a present one is read for its four members in order (`protected`, `enc`, `ct`, `sig`), and one that is not an object, or lacks a member or holds one that is not a string, is `envelope_invalid` naming it (`envelope is required`, `envelope.sig is required`). `pins` absent or null is none; a pin is read for `root`, `endpoint`, `leaf`, `state` and `leaf_fingerprint` in that order, and one that is not an object or lacks a required member, or holds one of the wrong type, is `bad_request` naming it by its path (`pins[0] is required`, `pins[0].root is required`). A chain in the plaintext with a member that is not a string, or does not read as base64url, is `envelope_invalid` `plaintext shape`, as in `decide`. The first pin for the chain's root is the one read, as `decide` reads a node's pins; a pin whose leaf does not read is an error of the call in its reader's class (`parse`; `unsupported` for a key outside the profile), never `superseded leaf`. |

Validate to the pinned root and the dialed address, and follow only when the chain is newer than or equal to the pin. |

**Plaintext shapes.** A request plaintext is `{"method", "params", "chain" | "leaf"}`. A result
plaintext is `{"result": <object>, "chain" | "leaf"}` or `{"error": {"code", "message", "data"?},
"chain" | "leaf"}` — the responder's proof beside the result, as §13.2 requires; the wrapper is the
clarification this library fixes and Phase 0.5 folds into the spec.

### 5.1 `decide` — the receiving rules as one pure function

`decide` implements SPEC §13.3 in order, §6.1 tiers, §5.3 new addresses with the removal tombstone,
§14.3 and §14.4, over state the host supplies. It changes nothing; it returns what it decided and the
effects the host must apply. `envelope.mjs receive()` is its specification, line for line.

Its arguments are the host's, decoded by the host, so a fault in them fails the call (`bad_request`)
and is never a decision about the peer: `node`, `envelope` and `now` absent or null, in that order
(`<name> is required`); then the node read whole as `NodeState` says, then the envelope's four
members in order, each named by its path when it is absent, null or not the type it is
(`node.pins[0].leaf is required`, `envelope.sig is required`); then `now`.

Input:

```json
{
  "now": "2026-09-13T12:00:00Z",
  "envelope": {"protected": "…", "enc": "…", "ct": "…", "sig": "…"},
  "node": {
    "endpoint": "https://agent.bharat.example/mcp",
    "accept_new_hosts": "auto" | "ask",
    "chain": ["<leaf>", "<root>"],
    "keys": [{"kid": "sha256:…", "leaf": "<leaf der>", "pkcs8": "…", "current": true}],
    "former": ["sha256:…"],
    "sibling_kids": ["sha256:…"],
    "pins": [{"root": "sha256:…", "endpoint": "https://…", "leaf": "<leaf der>", "state": "active" | "pending_out" | "blocked", "leaf_fingerprint"?: "sha256:…"}],
    "tombstones": [{"root": "sha256:…", "leaf": "<leaf der>", "at": "2026-…"}],
    "former_endpoints": [{"root": "sha256:…", "endpoint": "https://…", "at": "2026-…"}],
    "seen": ["msg-id", "…"]
  }
}
```

`keys` are the leaves this endpoint holds for the identity served at the path the envelope arrived
at: the current one and superseded ones the host keeps until their `notAfter` (the core drops a
non-current key past its `notAfter` itself). `former` are the key ids of leaves once held and no
longer, for `certificate_renewed`. `sibling_kids` are the key ids held for *other* identities on the
same origin, so a key held for another identity is `envelope_invalid`, never answered with a chain.

Output:

```json
{
  "result": {"code": "ok", "tier": "contact" | "pending" | "guest" | "pending_new_address",
             "root": "sha256:…", "endpoint": "https://…", "method": "tools/call", "tool": "send_message",
             "params": {…}, "form": "chain" | "leaf", "leaf": "<leaf der the signature verified under>",
             "replayed"?: true, "why"?: "unknown root" | "blocked" | "superseded leaf", "demote"?: false | true,
             "address_claim"?: "sha256:…", "forced"?: "tombstone", "decision"?: "ask"},
  "effects": [
    {"op": "seen", "msg_id": "…"},
    {"op": "pin_update", "root": "…", "endpoint": "…", "leaf": "…"},
    {"op": "former_endpoint", "root": "…", "endpoint": "…", "at": "…"},
    {"op": "event", "event": "new_address" | "renewal", "root": "…", "endpoint"?: "…"},
    {"op": "pending", "root": "…", "endpoint": "…", "leaf": "<leaf der>", "why": "ask" | "returned after removal"}
  ]
}
```

The other results, each with an empty `effects` list unless stated: `{"code": "envelope_invalid",
"why"}` — and when `why` is `guest may only redeem or request` it also carries `root` and `leaf`, so a
host holding an older pin of that leaf's key learns the root above it (§14.3) and decides again; `{"code": "chain_required"}`; `{"code": "certificate_renewed", "data": {"chain": [...]}}`;
`{"code": "pending_approval"}`; and `{"code": "ok", "replayed": true}` for a seen `msg_id`.
The `why` strings are the seed's, verbatim, so the intrusion suite reads both ports alike.

Order, as `receive()` has it (freshness also refuses `exp − ts` over 30 days, §13.1, as `exp too far from ts`): decode `protected` → header members exactly `cty,exp,kid,msg_id,suite,ts,v`
→ their types (`v`, `ts`, `exp` integers, the rest strings, else `header member types`)
→ `v` = 2 and a known suite → `kid` held (current, or superseded and not past `notAfter`), else a
sibling's → `envelope_invalid`, a former → `certificate_renewed`, unknown → `envelope_invalid` → suite
fits the held leaf's key → `enc` is exactly the suite's `Npk`, 65 or 32 (`encapsulated key is not the suite's length`: `sig` covers the three members concatenated, so the length is what fixes the boundary) → HPKE open → plaintext members exactly `chain,method,params` or
`leaf,method,params`, method `tools/call` or `tools/list` → **small form**: leaf fingerprint matched
against pins not blocked, the held leaf within validity, `sig` verifies, else `chain_required` in every
case; then freshness (`cty` is a call, `now < exp`, `|now − ts| ≤ 300 s`, non-empty `msg_id`, replay) →
tier by pin state → **full form**: `validate_chain` at `now` with no expectation (`envelope_invalid`
with `chain rule N: reason`), `sig` under the chain's leaf key, freshness; root unpinned → tombstone
within 30 days with a newer leaf → `pending_new_address` forced `ask`, else guest; guest binding: the
method is `tools/call`, the tool `redeem_invite` or `request_contact`, `params.arguments.card`
decodes, its certificate byte-equals the chain's leaf, the endpoint is not this node's own
(`guest endpoint is this node's own address`, §14.5), `address_claim` names a pin at that endpoint
or a former endpoint within 30 days; root pinned and blocked → guest; superseded → guest (a guest's
answer carries `why`, one of `unknown root`, `blocked` and `superseded leaf`, and `demote`, true for
the last two: a pin for the root stands and the caller is a guest anyway, so a host resolves it to no
contact row — the host reads `demote`, never the words); conflict →
`envelope_invalid`; another endpoint → `ask` pending or `auto` re-pin with the former endpoint recorded
and a `new_address` event; newer at the pinned endpoint → `pin_update` and a `renewal` event; then
`pending_out` allows `tools/list` and `contact_accepted`/`contact_rejected` at tier `pending` (a listing
names no tool, and answers at the tier the caller earns, SPEC §6, §13.2), else `pending_approval`; else
contact.

A `pending_new_address` result is the host's to answer as SPEC §5.3 words it: the `update_contact` that
brought the new address answers `{"status": "pending"}`; every other call from that address, until the
owner decides, answers `pending_approval`.

## 6. Vault (SPEC §9; the format shared by the wallet page and the CLI)

A wallet keeps two sealed documents, and both are this envelope:

```json
{"format": "pact-vault/1",
 "kdf": {"name": "argon2id", "m_kib": 65536, "t": 3, "p": 1},
 "salt": "<b64url 16>", "nonce": "<b64url 12>", "ct": "<b64url>"}
```

The key is Argon2id(passphrase, salt) → 32 bytes; the cipher is AES-256-GCM; the AAD is the RFC 8785
canonical JSON of the document without `ct`. The **file** is the root and nothing else — the person's
backup, sealed under the recovery key (in a wallet without a credential, the passphrase the person
chose), written once when the root is made and again only when the root is re-bound or a hardware key
takes it; a wallet never writes a leaf, a ledger entry or a contact into it. A root entry carries its
key (`pkcs8`), names the card that holds it (`holder`), or both — a key imported to a card and kept:

```json
{"v": 2,
 "roots": [{"fingerprint", "cn", "alg"?, "pkcs8"?, "holder"?, "cert", "created"}],
 "prf"?: "<b64url 32: the §2.1 secret, for a derived root>",
 "passkey"?: {"credential_id"}}
```

The **record** is the ledger and the contact book — under the store key of §2.1 for a wallet with a
credential, beside the file under the recovery key for one without — and the roots without their
keys, or with one once a root has been re-bound:

```json
{"v": 2,
 "roots"?: [{"fingerprint", "cn", "cert", "created", "pkcs8"?, "rebound_at"?}],
 "ledger": [{"root", "endpoint", "not_before", "not_after", "issued_at", "origin"?}],
 "contacts": [{"root", "endpoint", "name", "leaf"?, "root_cert"?, "added"}],
 "passkey"?: {"credential_id"}, "backup_verified_at"?: <ms>}
```

A ledger entry is the endpoint and the dates, never the leaf: that is the host's to serve and grants
nothing. `v` is 2 at both ends — `vault_seal` refuses anything else as `bad_request`, and `vault_open`
refuses a document that opens to an earlier generation as `vault` — and nothing converts.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vault_seal` | `passphrase`: string, `plaintext`, `kdf`?: KdfArgs, `salt`?: B64url, `nonce`?: B64url | `vault`: VaultDocument<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `vault` | `plaintext` is a VaultPlaintext or a RecordPlaintext, and its `v` is 2: anything else is `bad_request` (`a vault plaintext is v 2: the root, or the record`). That generation is all `vault_seal` checks of the plaintext (and `vault_open` of what it opens): the two shapes are held by `wallet_issue`, where the rules read them, so a stricter seal or open cannot lock a person out of a document a wallet already keeps. Read in this order: `passphrase` (absent: `passphrase is required`; empty: `empty passphrase`), `plaintext` and its generation, then `kdf`, `salt` and `nonce`, then the nonce's length (`vault`, `nonce is 12 bytes`) and the salt's (`vault`, `salt is at least 8 bytes`: `VaultSaltMin`). `kdf` absent or null is `KdfDefault`, and one that is not an object is `bad_request` `kdf is required`. An object is read by the one reader `vault_open` reads a document's `kdf` with, except that a member left out takes the default: a `name` other than `argon2id`, or one that is not a string, is `vault` `unknown kdf`; a parameter that is not a whole number written as one (`1.0`, `-0`, `"8192"`), or is outside its range, is `vault` `kdf parameters out of range`, never truncated; and a member other than those four, named in any case but theirs, is `vault` `kdf holds name, m_kib, t and p, and nothing else: <member>`. `salt` and `nonce` are for tests only. |
| `vault_open` | `passphrase`: string, `vault` | `plaintext`<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `vault` | Read in this order: `vault` (absent or null: `vault is required`), `passphrase` (absent: `passphrase is required`), then the document's header, where it does not read, all `vault`: a document that is not an object, or whose `format` is not `pact-vault/1`, is `not a pact-vault/1 document`; its `kdf` is read by the one reader `vault_seal`'s is, with all four members (`Kdf`): one that is not an object, or whose `name` is absent, not a string or not `argon2id`, is `unknown kdf`, a parameter that is absent, not a whole number written as one, or outside its range is `kdf parameters out of range`, and another member is `kdf holds name, m_kib, t and p, and nothing else: <member>`; `salt`, `nonce` and `ct` that are absent or not strings are no bytes, and one that is not base64url, or a nonce that is not 12 bytes, is the one message below; then a salt under `VaultSaltMin` bytes is `salt is at least 8 bytes`. A wrong passphrase and a tampered document are one message (`the passphrase is wrong or the vault is damaged`). A document that opens to a plaintext whose `v` is not 2 was written by an earlier wallet and is refused (`vault`, `this vault was written by an earlier wallet and is not opened: there is no conversion`); nothing converts. |
| `wallet_issue` | `vault_plaintext`: VaultPlaintext, `record_plaintext`: RecordPlaintext, `root_fingerprint`: string, `csr`: Csr, `now`: InstantIn, `valid_days`?: integer, `move`?: boolean | `der`: CertDer, `endpoint`: string, `not_before`: Instant, `not_after`: Instant, `ledger_entry`: LedgerEntry, `new_host`: boolean, `warnings`: [string]<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` | Two documents, as §9 keeps them: the vault is the root and nothing else, the record holds the ledger this reads and the entry answered is appended to. A vault carrying `ledger` or `contacts` is refused (`bad_request`, `a vault holds the root and nothing else: its ledger and contacts belong in the record`); an absent or null document is `vault_plaintext is required` or `record_plaintext is required` (CONTRACT §0), and a record that is not an object `record_plaintext is required: the ledger lives there`. After `root_fingerprint`, `csr`, `now` and `valid_days` (present and not an integer: `valid_days is required`), each document is held to its schema before anything in it is read, as follows. The vault: not an object, `vault_plaintext is required: the root lives there`; then its `v`; then the first member, in sorted order, it does not hold, `vault_plaintext holds v, roots, prf and passkey, and nothing else: <member>`; then its `roots` (absent or not a list: `the vault's roots is a list`), each entry a `VaultRoot` (`the vault's root <i> does not read: <member>`: the first of `fingerprint`, `cn`, `cert` and `created` that is absent, not a string, not a fingerprint or not an instant, then an `alg`, `pkcs8`, `holder` or `rebound_at` of the wrong type, then the first member, in sorted order, it does not hold; an entry that is not an object, `the vault's root <i> does not read`); then its `prf` (32 bytes, or `the vault's prf does not read`) and its `passkey` (an object holding `credential_id`, a string, and nothing else, or `the vault's passkey does not read`). Then the record, likewise: `record_plaintext holds v, roots, ledger, contacts, passkey and backup_verified_at, and nothing else: <member>`; its `roots` where present, as the vault's (`the record's roots is a list`, `the record's root <i> does not read: <member>`); its `ledger` (not a list: `the record's ledger is a list`) and every ledger entry, every root's: an entry that is not an object, lacks a required member, has one of the wrong type, a `root` that is not a fingerprint, an empty `endpoint` or an instant that does not parse, or carries one it does not hold is refused (`the record's ledger entry <i> does not read: <member>`), never skipped — skipped, it could be the live leaf; its `contacts` (not a list: `the record's contacts is a list`), each entry a `VaultContact` (`the record's contact <i> does not read: <member>`: `root` absent or not a fingerprint, `endpoint` absent or not a string, a `name`, `leaf`, `root_cert` or `added` that is not a string or, for `added`, not an instant, then the first member, in sorted order, it does not hold; an entry that is not an object, `the record's contact <i> does not read`); its `passkey` (`the record's passkey does not read`) and its `backup_verified_at`, a whole number (`the record's backup_verified_at does not read`). A root with no `pkcs8` is refused (`this root is held on a card: wallet_issue signs only with a key the vault holds`), and one whose `pkcs8` does not read is refused in its reader's class (`parse`; `unsupported` for a key outside the profile). The entry answered is the endpoint and the dates, never the leaf. The wallet's rules: `csr_check` with the vault's roots as `root_spkis`; then `ledger_check`'s rules over the record's ledger (a record with no `ledger` has no entry to read): `new_host` true when no ledger entry names that endpoint's host, with the warning `new host: this endpoint's host has never been issued to`; the **live leaf is the newest one issued** (§14.3) and a second endpoint while it is unexpired is refused unless `move: true`, which instead warns `move: the live leaf at the previous endpoint is superseded once contacts see this one` (a `move` or a `move_back`); `not_before` monotonic over the ledger; `valid_days` absent means 365 and an explicit 0 is refused. |

Passphrases never appear in arguments of the CLI; the wallet page holds them in memory
only for the call, and an empty passphrase seals nothing (`bad_request`). What the core zeroizes
when a call returns: every private key it decoded, the PKCS #8 bytes it decoded them from, the
HPKE ephemeral, shared secret, key, nonce and the HMAC chaining buffers, the vault's derived key
and its decrypted bytes. What it does not: the JSON argument and answer strings — including a
`pkcs8` member and a vault's decoded plaintext as a JSON value — and wasm-bindgen's copies of
those strings in linear memory, which are freed but not cleared. A host that must not leave key
material behind treats the strings it passes and receives as its own to clear.

**The KDF's range, at both ends, on both paths.** `m_kib` 8192–2097152 (8 MiB–2 GiB), `t` 1–16, `p` 1–16, `name` `argon2id`; anything else is `{"error": "vault", "why": "kdf parameters out of range"}` (or `"unknown kdf"`), from `vault_seal` and `vault_open` alike, through one reader in each port, and every derivation — a typed call's too — is held to the same range. The parameters are read out of the document **before the passphrase is tested**, so an unbounded reader hands an attacker's file a 256 GiB allocation or a derivation that never returns, and an unbounded writer seals the person's root behind a KDF a laptop brute-forces. A value that does not fit in 32 bits is out of range, never truncated. A salt under `VaultSaltMin` (8 bytes) is `{"error": "vault", "why": "salt is at least 8 bytes"}` at both ends, named before Argon2id is asked for anything: no `why` is the library's.

### 6.1 The ledger — what signing would mean

`ledger_check` is SPEC §9's issuance rules over the record's ledger, answered as facts and not as
prose: whether a leaf is live and where, whether this endpoint or its host has been issued to, the
`notBefore` the next leaf must follow, and which move notice applies (`renew`, `move`, `new_host`,
`move_back`, or `no_ledger` when the signer has no record to read). `wallet_issue` applies these
rules; the `pact` CLI applies them to a card-held root, where there is no key to hand the core; a
wallet page and a host render the notice from them. Every entry is read before any rule is, and one
that does not read is refused, never skipped.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ledger_check` | `ledger`?: array\|null, `root`: Fingerprint, `endpoint`: string, `now`: InstantIn, `move`?: boolean | `refusal`: string\|null, `new_host`: boolean, `known_endpoint`: boolean, `previous_not_before`: Instant \| null, `live`: `endpoint`: string, `not_after`: Instant \| null, `notice`: `kind`: renew\|move\|new_host\|move_back\|no_ledger, `from`?: string, `until`?: Instant<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | The wallet's ledger rules, as facts, in the one place they are written: `wallet_issue` applies them, the `pact` CLI applies them for a card-held root, and a wallet page or a host renders the move notice from them. In order: `root` (absent or empty: `root is required`), `endpoint`, `now`, `move` (present and not a boolean: `move is required`); then `endpoint` not in normal form is refused (`endpoint is not an https URL in normal form`); then every ledger entry, every root's, is read as `wallet_issue` reads it (`the record's ledger is a list`; `the record's ledger entry <i> does not read: <member>`, a `root` that is not a fingerprint and an empty `endpoint` included) — an entry that does not read is REFUSED, a `not_before` that does not parse included, never skipped: skipped, it could be the live leaf. The **live leaf** is this root's newest entry by `not_before` (§14.3; the first of equals, in ledger order), if its `not_after` is after `now`; an older entry still in its validity is history, not live. `notice.kind`: with no ledger, `no_ledger`; a leaf live at another endpoint, `move_back` when this endpoint has been issued to before and `move` when it has not (both with `from` and `until`, the live leaf's endpoint and `not_after`); otherwise `renew` when this endpoint has been issued to, and `new_host` when it has not. The kind does not depend on `move`; only `refusal` does. |

### 6.2 The export (SPEC §9.2)

An export is one unencrypted zip — `manifest.json`, `contacts.csv`, `threads.csv`, `messages.jsonl`,
`media/<sha256>` — and a wallet's book is one holding the manifest and `contacts.csv` only. The core
never opens a zip: a host reads the container and hands over what it read, and every rule that can
be decided on that is decided here, once. Every refusal of what a file holds, or of rows to write,
is `bad_request`, and its `why` begins with where: the member, then the row (the header is row 1) or
the line, then the column or member. An argument that is not an instant (`now`, `exported_at`) is
`parse`, as everywhere in this contract.

**Reading.** The host passes `export_read` the central directory and the three text members, then
streams `messages.jsonl` through `export_read_messages` in batches of lines (`first_line` numbering
them in the whole member), then checks each media file, then calls `export_read_end`. What only
the host can do, and the words both hosts of this repository use for it (the Go port's
`ReadExportZip` and the `pact` CLI):

- count the bytes it actually decompresses, never the sizes a header states: a text member over its
  bound is `<member>: over <n> bytes`, a line `messages.jsonl: line <n>: over 65536 bytes`, a media
  file `media/<h>: over 5242880 bytes`, and the whole file over the host's own ceiling `the file is
  over the <n>-byte ceiling this host sets`;
- refuse a member that is not UTF-8 text (`<member>: not UTF-8 text`, or `messages.jsonl: line <n>:
  not UTF-8 text`) and one that does not decompress (`<member>: does not decompress`);
- hash `messages.jsonl` as it streams it, and each media file against its own name (`media/<h>: its
  sha256 is not its name`): the manifest lists the text members only, and a media member is bound
  by its name and counted by `counts.media` (SPEC 2.2.2);
- refuse a media file whose bytes are a private key — PKCS #8 or SEC1 in DER, or text holding one
  (`media/<h>: holds a private key`);
- hand `export_read_end` the media `export_read` answered, so a media file no message names is
  refused.

**Writing.** `export_write` answers the canonical `contacts.csv` and `threads.csv` and a partial
manifest; `export_write_messages` answers the lines; `export_manifest` finishes the manifest with
the host's count and hash of `messages.jsonl`. The bytes are the same from every port: a Go host and
a Rust host that write the same rows write the same file. A media file is stored, not recompressed.
What a contact controls never stops the export (SPEC 9.2#22–25): `export_write_messages` leaves out
a message whose body is a private key and answers it in `left_out`, and a host that writes in
batches names the file's msg_ids in `msg_ids`, so a reply to a message not carried is written null.
The core never sees a media file's bytes, so the host checks each before it writes: a message whose
file is a private key is left out with the file and listed with the rest, for the host to report to
the person.
`book_rows` is the one mapping from the wallet's own book (`VaultContact`, §6) to those rows, which
every wallet uses before `export_write` writes a book.

The Go port also offers two conveniences over these functions, which are not contract functions and
which its own tests run against the whole corpus: `ReadExportZip` (the reading above, with
`archive/zip`) and `WriteExportZip`, which runs the reader's rules on what it is handed before it
writes the first byte. The fixture corpus is `go/exportcorpus/`: two valid exports (one whose local
headers disagree with its central directory), a valid book, and hostile files, each naming the
refusal it must produce (`go/exportcorpus/cases.json`); both ports' tests and `js/parity.mjs` read
all of it. Its files name one fixed owner; `pact vectors corpus --owner <root> --out <dir>` writes
the same corpus for another root, each file with its defect and `cases.json` with the same
refusals, so a host can import every file into an identity it holds. Read-side parity cases on the core's functions (`js/cases/export-reader.mjs`) reach
rules that no file does.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `export_read` | `directory`: [DirectoryEntry], `manifest`?: string, `contacts_csv`?: string, `threads_csv`?: string, `owner`: Fingerprint, `now`: InstantIn | `contacts`: [ContactRow], `threads`: [ThreadRow], `media`: [`hash`: Sha256Hex, `size`: integer]<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | SPEC §9.2's validation of everything but the messages and the media bytes, refusing the whole file at the first fault; every refusal of the file is `bad_request` whose `why` names the member, then the row (the header is row 1) and the column. In order: each directory entry, in the order given (a name that is not exactly `manifest.json`, `contacts.csv`, `threads.csv`, `messages.jsonl`, `media/` or `media/` and 64 lowercase hex: `entry "<name>": not a name an export holds`; `appears twice`; `encrypted`; a symbolic link; a directory but `media/`; a stated size over its bound); `manifest.json` and `contacts.csv` present; the manifest (exactly its members, `pact_export` 2, `owner` a fingerprint and the importing identity's, the counts whole numbers, `owner_name` and `tool` holding no private key, `files` naming only the text members — `contacts.csv`, `threads.csv`, `messages.jsonl` — each a lowercase hex sha256, never a media member, which is bound by its name and counted (SPEC 2.2.2)); every text member but the manifest listed in `files`, and every listed member present; `threads.csv`, `messages.jsonl` and `media/` present when counted; the media entries as many as counted; `contacts.csv` (its sha256, its header exactly, at most 5000 rows, each row's cells — a cell that holds a private key is refused before its column's rule — the root a fingerprint, unique, not the owner; the endpoint in normal form and passing the address guard; names at most 200 characters; the status; `true` or `false`; §8's permissions, single-spaced, none twice; the leaf a leaf and the root certificate a root of §14.1's profile, the latter for the row's root; `added` an instant) and its count; then `threads.csv` the same way (ids unique, the contact a root in `contacts.csv`). One leading `'` is stripped from every cell. A row's `leaf` is answered only when `[leaf, root_cert]` validates at the row's endpoint at `now` (§14.2); otherwise it is null and pins nothing. `media` is each media member's hash and stated size, sorted by hash: the host checks each file's bytes against both as it streams it. |
| `export_read_messages` | `lines`: [string], `threads`: [string], `contacts`: [Fingerprint], `media`: [Sha256Hex], `first_line`?: integer | `messages`: [MessageRow], `media_seen`: [Sha256Hex]<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | One batch of messages.jsonl's lines as the host streams it (each line without its `\n`). Each line: at most 65536 bytes, one JSON object, exactly the members of a message (a stranger first, then a missing one), no member holding a private key, then each member's rule: `id` and `msg_id` not empty, `thread` and `contact` naming the file's, `direction`, `sender`, `time`, `body` at most 16384 bytes, `reply_to` a msg_id or null, `status`, and `attachments` at most one, each exactly `{file, filename, mime, size}` naming a media member; a message with an attachment has an empty body. A refusal is `messages.jsonl: line <n>, member <m>: <why>`. What only the whole member can decide is export_read_end's. |
| `export_read_end` | `manifest`: string, `messages_sha256`?: Sha256Hex \| null, `lines`: integer, `ids`: [string], `msg_ids`: [string], `reply_tos`: [string], `media_seen`: [Sha256Hex], `media`: [Sha256Hex] | `ok`: true<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | SPEC §9.2's rules across the whole of messages.jsonl, once it is streamed: the line count against `counts.messages`, the member's sha256 against `files`, `id` unique in the file, every `reply_to` naming a `msg_id` in the file, and every media member (`media`, the hashes export_read answered) named by some attachment (`media/<h>: nothing names it`). `lines` absent or null is `lines is required`, and one that is not a whole number `lines is a whole number`. |
| `export_write` | `owner`: Fingerprint, `owner_name`: string, `exported_at`: InstantIn, `tool`: string, `contacts`: [ContactRow], `threads`?: [ThreadRow], `media`?: [`hash`: Sha256Hex, `size`: integer] | `partial`: ExportManifest, `contacts_csv`: string, `threads_csv`: string\|null<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | The canonical members, the same bytes from every port: each row checked by the reader's rules (`contacts[<i>], column <c>: <why>`), contacts sorted by root and threads by id, a permission list sorted, instants written as RFC 3339 UTC seconds, every cell that begins with `=` `+` `-` `@` `'` a tab or a carriage return written with one `'` before it, a cell quoted exactly when it holds `,` `"` CR or LF, CRLF after every record. What a contact controls never stops the export (SPEC §9.2): `their_permissions` keeps only the names of §8, once each, and `display_name` is cut to 200 characters, on a character; the reader refuses both as written by anyone else. `owner_name` or `tool` holding a private key is refused, naming the member (`owner_name holds a private key`). The manifest's `files` lists the text members only; the media are counted. A book is this with no threads and no media. |
| `export_write_messages` | `messages`: [MessageRow], `msg_ids`?: [string] | `lines`: [string], `left_out`: [`id`: string, `reason`: string]<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | One line per message, in the order given, as RFC 8785 JSON; each message held to the reader's rules but its references, which the host holds (`messages[<i>], member <m>: <why>`). What a contact controls never stops the export (SPEC §9.2): a message whose `body` holds what reads as a private key is left out, not refused, and listed in `left_out` (`its body holds what reads as a private key, which an export never carries`) — the host leaves out the file it carried too; and a `reply_to` naming a message the file does not carry (not among `msg_ids`, or, without them, not among the messages written) is written `null`. Key material in any other member is refused. The host writes each line followed by `\n`, hashes the member's bytes and counts its lines for export_manifest. |
| `export_manifest` | `partial`: ExportManifest, `hashes`?: `messages.jsonl`?: Sha256Hex, `messages`?: integer | `manifest`: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | export_write's partial manifest finished with what the host counted and hashed: held to the manifest's rules first, refused if it already counts or lists messages, `messages.jsonl` required in `hashes` when there are messages. |
| `export_merge` | `held`: [ContactRow], `rows`: [ContactRow] | `write`: [ContactRow], `keep`: [Fingerprint], `conflicts`: [`root`: Fingerprint, `field`: endpoint\|leaf\|root_cert\|status\|permissions, `held`, `row`]<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | SPEC §9.2's import step 2: an imported leaf never replaces a pin the host validated itself (§14.5). A row whose root is not held is written; a row whose root is held WITHOUT a leaf is written when the row carries one (export_read kept it only because it validated); and what the person decided about that contact stays as held: a blocked contact stays blocked, and its `permissions` stay the ones granted. Every other held root is kept as held. Each of the endpoint, leaf and root certificate a row would change, and each of the `status` and `permissions` (a list compared as a set), is a conflict for the host to show. |
| `book_rows` | `contacts`: [VaultContact], `exported_at`: InstantIn | `rows`: [ContactRow]<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | The wallet's book as rows of contacts.csv, the one mapping every wallet uses (SPEC §9.2: a book is an export of contacts only). Each contact, in order: an object (`contacts[<i>] is an object`), no member but `root`, `endpoint`, `name`, `leaf`, `root_cert` and `added` (the first other, in sorted order: `contacts[<i>]: "<m>" is not a member of a wallet contact`), `root` and `endpoint` strings (`contacts[<i>]: <m> is required`), the rest strings when present (`contacts[<i>]: <m> is a string`). A row carries the root, the endpoint, the name (empty when absent), the leaf and the root certificate (null when absent), and `added` (the export's time when absent); its other columns are what a contact the wallet keeps is: an empty `display_name`, `status` `active`, `was_active` true, and nothing granted either way. The rows are not checked here: export_write holds each to the reader's rules. |

### 6.3 The call budgets (SPEC §12)

SPEC §12's per-caller budgets as one decision, for the check a host runs after it has opened an
envelope and knows the caller (layer 2 of pact-gateway `docs/release/two-layer-limits-2026-09-28.md`;
layer 1, per address and per path, is the host's edge). The rules are a document the host keeps in
its configuration and checks with `limits_rules_check` before it publishes one; the library holds no
default. The counters are rows the host keeps, handed in as `state` and handed back as `writes`: the
library does no I/O and reads no clock. A call is charged to every bucket of its charge or to none,
and the bucket keys are the cloud's `rate_buckets` keys, so rows written before the move read the
same after it. The arithmetic is the cloud's `RateLimiter.take`, operation for operation;
`js/cases/limits-vectors.json`, generated by running that TypeScript over SQLite
(`js/limits-vectors.mjs`), holds every port to its decisions and to the bits of every row it wrote.
Two rules have no TypeScript to be held to: the guest total, charged before the open, and the cap on
waiting requests.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `limits_rules_check` | `rules` | `ok`: true<br>or `ok`: false, `why`: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | Whether a rules document can be enforced as written, and the first reason it cannot, in this order: not an object (`the limits rules are an object`); a member it does not hold, the first in sorted order (`the limits rules hold <members>, and nothing else: <member>`); each member in the order of `LimitsRules`, absent or not a number (`<member> is a number`); then every number finite, `contact_calls_per_second` above 0 (`… is above 0`) and every other at least 1 (`… is at least 1`); `pending_in_cap` whole (`pending_in_cap is a whole number`); and a contact's bucket refilling from empty within the hour (`contact_burst / contact_calls_per_second is at most 3600: …`). `rules` absent or null is `bad_request`, `rules is required`. A host publishes no document this refuses. |
| `limits_decide` | `rules`: LimitsRules, `charge`: LimitsCharge, `now`: integer, `state`?: object\|null | `allowed`: boolean, `retry_after`: integer\|null, `refused_by`: string\|null, `writes`: [`bucket`: string, `tokens`: number, `updated_at`: integer]<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | SPEC §12's call budgets as one decision (crates/pact-limits; go/limits.go). A call is charged one token in EVERY bucket of its charge, or in none: a refusal spends nothing. A bucket's level is `min(burst, tokens + elapsed × rate)`, `elapsed` the seconds since `updated_at` and never negative (a clock that went back refills nothing, and the row is written with the earlier time); a level under 1 refuses, with `retry_after = max(1, ceil((1 − level) / rate))`. The arithmetic is the cloud's `RateLimiter.take` operation for operation in IEEE double precision, and `js/cases/limits-vectors.json` holds the two to the same decisions and the same bits. A host may delete a row idle for over an hour: under rules `limits_rules_check` passes it is full, and no decision changes. In order: `rules` (absent: `rules is required`; not enforceable: `the limits rules cannot be enforced: <limits_rules_check's why>`), `charge` (not an object: `charge is required`; `charge.kind is required`; `charge.kind is one of …`; a member its kind does not hold, the first in sorted order: `a <kind> charge holds <members>, and nothing else: <member>`; `charge.<member> is required` for a string that is absent or empty, `charge.<member> is a whole number` for a count, `charge.root is a string or null`, `charge.source is required`, `charge.addressed is required`), `now` (absent or null: `now is required`; otherwise `now is a time in milliseconds`: a whole number from 0 to 2^53 − 1, written without a fraction or an exponent), `state` (not an object: `state is an object of rows by bucket`; a row, in sorted order of key, that does not read: `the state's row <key> does not read: <member>`). |

## 7. Gates

1. `cargo test` and `go test ./...` each: rebuild the seven vector certificates byte for byte from
   `leaf_keys_pkcs8_hex` and the labelled seeds (root keys are derived from `seed("root/alina")` etc.,
   exactly as `gen.mjs`), prove every chain case, newest-leaf case, `certificate_renewed` case and
   `v: 2` envelope, and reproduce the three envelopes' `enc`/`ct` from their ephemeral seeds.
2. `js/check.mjs` runs the same proof through a port in Node, reading vectors from SPEC.md as the
   seed's `check.mjs` does: `--port wasm` (default) or `--port go`. **Both**, because for a long time
   only the first was run and the second was failing three assertions unseen — the three that re-seal
   a vector from its ephemeral seed and compare the bytes, which is the only check proving a port's
   envelopes are the vectors' envelopes.
3. `js/intrude.mjs` replays every scenario of `pact-protocol/vectors/intrude.mjs` with Mallory built
   on the seed library and the defender on a port: `--port wasm` (default) or `--port go`. Every
   scenario's verdict must match the seed's: blocked, residual, never REPRODUCES — and the run fails
   if the two suites do not hold the same scenarios, so neither side's count is written down here.
4. `node --test contract/schema.test.mjs` holds the contract's own validator to a value per keyword
   that must fail it, and asserts it REFUSES a keyword it does not implement — a validator that
   ignored one would let `contract.json` state a constraint nothing holds, which is worse than
   stating nothing.
5. `js/parity.mjs` is a **gate**, not a courtesy. It feeds both ports the same arguments — a missing
   member, a member that is `null`, bytes that will not decode, an explicit `valid_days: 0`, a
   mismatched `sig_alg`, a name that straddles the vCard fold, every private and loopback spelling of
   an address, a root offered as a key id — and compares the whole answer, `why` strings included.
   The vectors prove the bytes a peer sees; this proves the codes, the words and the shapes a
   *caller* sees, which no vector carries. Besides the cases written by hand, `js/cases/generated.mjs`
   makes, for every function this file declares, the shapes of a caller's mistake from the function's
   own `params`: `{}`; the hostile object `js/cases/hostile.json` (which the Go port's
   `TestCallNeverPanics` sweeps with too); each required member absent and `null`, held to §0's
   `<name> is required`; each optional string `""`; each optional member of the wrong type; a member
   the contract does not declare; and, for read order, each required member absent beside each other
   member of the wrong type. Each is varied from a call that succeeds on both ports, named per
   function. Until the audit of 2026-09-29 is fixed, the cases that fail today are listed in
   `js/cases/known-divergences.json`, each with the finding that closes it, and excused only while
   they fail exactly as listed; the list can only shrink. It also fails when:
   - the two dispatchers and `contract/contract.json` stop naming the same set of functions
     (`version` lived in one dispatcher and not the other until this check existed; a function
     described in the contract and dispatched by neither port would be prose nothing runs);
   - an answer does not hold to the shape the contract declares for it, from EITHER port — the one
     check here that two agreeing ports cannot pass by agreeing, since a member both grew, or both
     dropped, is invisible to a comparison;
   - a function on either dispatcher has no case here, so the contract cannot grow past its guard;
   - an error code a function declares is never produced by both ports in one case they answered
     alike — a refusal nobody compared, or a code nothing can reach, which is a claim to take out of
     this file;
   - a function is only ever compared through a list of named keys rather than whole. That last one
     is the point: `card_decode` dropped its entire `leaf` member in one port, and a key list would
     never have noticed, because a key list only looks at the keys someone thought to name. Where an
     answer carries something genuinely per-run — a random serial, a fresh ephemeral — the case
     passes a function that replaces that one value with a description of it, and everything else is
     still compared. Narrowing a case to `['error']` to make a disagreement go away is not a fix: a
     differing `why` *is* the finding.
6. `wasm-bindgen-test` in headless Chrome for the browser build. A host that runs `pkg-web` in a
   Worker or a page tests it there, in its own repository, against the bytes it vendored.

---

## Appendix: the domain types

Generated from `contract/contract.json`'s `$defs`, which is where the tables above get their words.
A type used in an argument and in an answer is one definition, which is the point of having the
file: `Fingerprint` cannot mean `sha256:…` in one function's row and something else in another's.

| Type | Shape | |
|---|---|---|
| `ErrorCode` | bad_request\|parse\|unsupported\|envelope_invalid\|vault\|key\|internal | Why a call failed. `bad_request`: an argument is missing or unusable as asked. `parse`: bytes that are there and will not read. `unsupported`: an algorithm or a function this library does not have. `envelope_invalid`: SPEC §12's code, for an envelope that does not open or prove itself. `vault`: the vault refused. `key` and `internal` are declared so a caller's switch has a name for them; no input known reaches either. |
| `B64url` | string | Bytes, as base64url without padding. An ANSWER always spells them this way. An ARGUMENT is read forgivingly about padding and the standard alphabet, and about nothing else: whitespace of any kind is refused (§0). The members of an envelope that travelled are not read forgivingly at all (§5). |
| `Alg` | ed25519\|p256 | A key algorithm. A key of any other is refused where it is read (CONTRACT §0). |
| `Fingerprint` | string | `"sha256:" + b64url(SHA-256(SPKI))`. |
| `Instant` | string | An RFC 3339 UTC instant with second precision, as every answer writes one. |
| `InstantIn` | string | An RFC 3339 UTC instant as an argument, in the one grammar every port reads (SPEC 2.2.2): upper-case T and Z, no offset, `.` alone before a fraction of a second, which is allowed and DROPPED, because the boundary is whole seconds. |
| `Pkcs8` | B64url | A private key: PKCS #8 DER. |
| `Spki` | B64url | A public key: SubjectPublicKeyInfo DER. |
| `CertDer` | B64url | One X.509 certificate, DER. |
| `Chain` | [CertDer] | `[leaf, root]`. |
| `Tbs` | B64url | A TBSCertificate, DER: the bytes an external signer signs. |
| `SigAlg` | B64url | An AlgorithmIdentifier, DER — the TBS's own third field. |
| `Csr` | B64url | A PKCS #10 CertificationRequest, DER. |
| `Serial` | B64url | A certificate serial number, 8 to 20 bytes. Absent, the core draws 8 random bytes. |
| `Seed32` | B64url | Exactly 32 bytes. |
| `Suite` | PACT-SEAL-P256\|PACT-SEAL-X25519 | An HPKE suite (§5). |
| `Form` | chain\|leaf | How the sender proves itself inside the plaintext: its whole chain, or the fingerprint of a leaf the recipient already holds. |
| `Key` | `alg`: Alg, `pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `spki`: Spki, `fingerprint`: Fingerprint |  |
| `Envelope` | `protected`: B64url, `enc`: B64url, `ct`: B64url, `sig`: B64url | A sealed envelope as this library WRITES one (SPEC §13.1). |
| `ArrivedEnvelope` | `protected`: string, `enc`: string, `ct`: string, `sig`: string | An envelope as it ARRIVED: four strings, which may be anything. Judging their spelling is the function's work, not the caller's. |
| `Certificate` | `kind`: root\|leaf\|other, `subject`: string, `issuer`: string, `serial`: B64url, `not_before`: Instant, `not_after`: Instant, `alg`: Alg, `spki`: Spki, `fingerprint`: Fingerprint, `key_id`: B64url, `ski`: B64url \| null, `aki`: B64url \| null, `ca`: boolean, `path_len`: integer\|null, `key_usage`: [integer], `eku`: [string], `uris`: [string], `dns`: [string], `sig_alg`: string, `extensions`: [`id`: string, `critical`: boolean], `profile_error`: string\|null, `bytes`: integer | A certificate read back. `profile_error` judges it as a root when it is self-issued and a CA, otherwise as a leaf. |
| `ChainAccepted` | `ok`: true, `leaf_spki`: Spki, `leaf_fingerprint`: Fingerprint, `root_fingerprint`: Fingerprint, `endpoint`: string, `not_before`: Instant, `not_after`: Instant, `alg`: Alg |  |
| `ChainRefused` | `ok`: false, `rule`: integer, `reason`: string |  |
| `Pin` | `root`: string, `endpoint`: string, `leaf`: string, `state`?: active\|pending_out\|blocked, `leaf_fingerprint`?: string | A contact as the host holds it. `state` absent is `active`. |
| `HeldKey` | `kid`: Fingerprint, `leaf`: CertDer, `pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `current`?: boolean |  |
| `Tombstone` | `root`: string, `leaf`: string, `at`: string |  |
| `FormerEndpoint` | `root`: string, `endpoint`: string, `at`: string |  |
| `Windows` | {"skew_s":300,"max_lifetime_s":2592000,"tombstone_s":2592000,"claim_window_s":2592000,"max_leaf_days":398,"signing_max_ahead_s":600} | The protocol's windows, in seconds unless named otherwise, as both ports hold them (a test in each holds its constants to these, and a host that needs one reads it here): `skew_s`, how far a received envelope's `ts` may be from now, and `max_lifetime_s`, the most `exp − ts` may be (SPEC §13.3); `tombstone_s`, how long a removal tombstone holds a returning root at `ask` (§5.3), and `claim_window_s`, how long an endpoint stays claimed by the root that was pinned at it (§5.2) — each an age strictly under the window; `max_leaf_days`, the longest leaf a verifier accepts (§14.2); `signing_max_ahead_s`, the furthest ahead a signing request may expire (§9.1). |
| `CanonicalNumbers` | [["1e21","1e+21"],["1.5e300","1.5e+300"],["1e-7","1e-7"],["0.000001","0.000001"],["100.0","100"],["9223372036854775808.0","9223372036854776000"],["1e20","100000000000000000000"],["0.1","0.1"],["-0.0","0"],["42","42"],["1e-5","0.00001"],["0.0000001","1e-7"],["1.25e-9","1.25e-9"],["-1e-7","-1e-7"],["1e100","1e+100"],["9007199254740992","9007199254740992"],["9007199254740993","9007199254740992"],["-9007199254740993","-9007199254740992"],["12345678901234567890","12345678901234567000"]] | How the canonical JSON of an envelope header and a vault's authenticated data writes a number (RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3: as ECMAScript's Number prints it). Each row is a JSON number as a caller may write it and the text both ports canonicalise it to; a test in each port runs every row. |
| `NodeState` | `endpoint`: string, `accept_new_hosts`?: auto\|ask, `chain`?: Chain, `keys`?: [HeldKey], `former`?: [string], `sibling_kids`?: [string], `pins`?: [Pin], `tombstones`?: [Tombstone], `former_endpoints`?: [FormerEndpoint], `seen`?: [string] | What the host knows, handed to `decide` whole. Every list absent is empty; `accept_new_hosts` absent is `auto`, and anything but `auto` or `ask` is refused (`node.accept_new_hosts is auto or ask`). Read member by member in this order, a held key as `kid`, `leaf`, `pkcs8`, `current`, a pin as `root`, `endpoint`, `leaf`, `state`, `leaf_fingerprint`, a tombstone as `root`, `leaf`, `at`, a former endpoint as `root`, `endpoint`, `at`: a member absent, null or of the wrong type where one is required is `bad_request` naming it by its path (`node.endpoint is required`, `node.keys[0].kid is required`, `node.seen[1] is required`). | `GuestWhy` | unknown root\|blocked\|superseded leaf | Why a caller proven by a chain is a guest: its root is not pinned (`unknown root`), its pin is blocked (`blocked`), or the leaf it signed with is older than the pinned one (`superseded leaf`, §14.3). The words are the seed's `receive()`'s. |

| `Kdf` | `name`: "argon2id", `m_kib`: integer, `t`: integer, `p`: integer | The key derivation, as a vault DOCUMENT carries it: all four members, each inside its range. The ranges are checked at both ends on both paths, by one parser — an unbounded reader hands an attacker's file a 256 GiB allocation, and an unbounded writer seals a person's root behind a KDF a laptop brute-forces. A value that does not fit in 32 bits is out of range, never truncated. |
| `KdfArgs` | `name`?: "argon2id", `m_kib`?: integer, `t`?: integer, `p`?: integer | The same, as an ARGUMENT to `vault_seal`: every member may be left out and takes `KdfDefault`'s, and what is given is held to the same range as a document's. |
| `KdfDefault` | {"name":"argon2id","m_kib":65536,"t":3,"p":1} | The key derivation `vault_seal` uses for a member its caller leaves out: 64 MiB, three passes, one lane. A test in each port holds its default to this, and its bounds to `Kdf`'s and `KdfArgs`'s. |
